evidence: M-O s.v. triangle: rectangular: quadrātum oblongum, from Mercuriale (1569): alia quadrātam, alia quadrātam oblongam, alia rotundiusculam, alia ōvālem
terms.comment: Mercuriale’s phrase, of the shapes of Roman bathtubs, and the plainest noun for the shape: a four-sided figure longer than it is wide. It is made of two classical words; Vitruvius sets quadrātus and oblongus side by side for square and rectangular buildings (see the examples), so for a child the adjective often does the work: Hoc nōn quadrātum est, sed oblongum.

terms.gloss: oblong, rectangular, longer than it is wide
evidence: Vitr. 5.2.1: sī quadrāta erit … sīn autem oblonga fuerit
terms.comment: Vitruvius’s word for a court or a hall that is not square; Lewis & Short notes it is not in Cicero or Caesar.

evidence: M-O s.v. triangle: rectangle, from Latham
terms.comment: The modern geometer’s word, from rēctus and angulus; not in Lewis & Short. The ē is long as in rēctus.

phrases.latin: Hoc nōn quadrātum est, sed oblongum: duo latera longiōra sunt.
phrases.english: This isn’t a square, it’s a rectangle: two of the sides are longer.

phrases.latin: Quā fōrmā est jānua? — Quadrātī oblongī.
phrases.english: What shape is the door? — A rectangle.

phrases.latin: In palaestrīs peristȳlia quadrāta sīve oblonga ita sint facienda, utī duōrum stadiōrum habeant ambulātiōnis circuitiōnem
phrases.english: In the wrestling schools the colonnaded courts, whether square or rectangular, should be built so that the walk round them is two stades long

phrases.latin: Jūgerī mēnsūram ducentōs et quadrāgintā longitūdinis pedēs esse dīmidiōque in lātitūdinem patēre nōn ferē quisquam est quī ignōret
phrases.english: There is hardly anyone who does not know that a iugerum is two hundred and forty feet long and half as much across
